content.text: When you lift an object, you do work against gravity. This work is stored as gravitational potential energy (GPE). The higher you lift it, the more energy is stored—energy that can be released when the object falls.
Gravitational potential energy is calculated using GPE = mgh. It depends on mass, gravitational field strength, and height above a reference point.
is the energy stored in an object due to its position in a gravitational field.
Depends on mass, height, and gravitational field strength
Is a form of potential energy (stored, ready to be released)
Can be converted to kinetic energy when the object falls
Requires a reference point (usually ground level)
Can be positive or negative depending on reference point
More massive objects have more GPE at the same height

GPE is relative to a chosen reference point. Always be clear about where you are measuring height from. On Earth, g is approximately 9.8 N/kg, but you may be told to use 10 N/kg in exam calculations.
"GPE is always measured from the ground"
— GPE depends on the reference point chosen. You can set zero GPE at any convenient level.
"Heavier objects fall faster, so they gain more KE"
— Without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate. Heavier objects have more GPE and KE, but the same speed.
— GPE only depends on vertical height. Whether you climb straight up or take a winding path, GPE change is the same.
"Work done lifting = force × total distance moved"
— Only the vertical component of displacement counts for GPE.
"Objects below the reference point have no GPE"
— They have negative GPE relative to that reference point.
